## Page 1: Prologo

### Full · `prologo.mp3` · 170 words

> Esteemed colleagues,
>
> I write to you from the village I told you of, where I arrived on the evening train with an umbrella that proved entirely useless. The parish priest, a kind and very tired man, handed me the keys to the old sacristy. Behind a walnut wardrobe was a door, crudely bricked up; behind the door, six crates of documents.
>
> Séance minutes, letters never sent, torn diary pages, cuttings from the local gazette, telegrams whose ink has long since faded to violet. They cover fifty years and three generations of a single family: scientists, or something they liked to call by that name, who for half a century tried to speak with the dead. And not, it would seem, always without an answer.
>
> I have resolved to sort and transcribe them before forming any judgement. The first document is the record of a wake. I ask you to read it as I did: with the scepticism the Society demands, and with the window shut.
>
> *Your most devoted, F. Halász*

> I am writing to you from the village I told you about. I arrived on the evening train, with an umbrella that did not help at all. Behind the door there were six crates full of documents.
>

## Page 2: G1Intro

### Full · `g1intro.mp3` · 234 words

> Father was buried on the Day of the Dead, under a thin rain that could not make up its mind to fall. The village came to the cemetery in good numbers, but stayed on the far side of the low wall: no one would go near the grave, and the gravedigger worked quickly, without looking in. It was said the old man had spent his last years shut up in the estate with machines that hummed through the night, and that from the windows of his laboratory there sometimes came a light of a colour no one could name.
>
> The heirs had arrived on the coach the evening before, each from a different city, each with a trunk and the same letter from the notary. The estate was theirs, and with it the debts, the instruments, the animals in their cages and Father's Journal: a leather-bound notebook swollen with notes, sketches and formulae. On the last page he had written there was a single sentence, underlined twice, so hard that the pen had cut the paper:
>
> *"Death is not a closed door: it is a veil. And veils can be lifted."*
>
> Father Anzelm blessed the body, closed his prayer book and told the heirs, loudly enough for everyone to hear, that he would pray for their souls with particular devotion.
>
> That night, in the estate, something began to knock on the walls.

## Page 3: G2Intro

### Full · `g2intro.mp3` · 131 words

> The second crate opens with a gap of seventeen years. The papers of the first generation stop in 1856; the next begin in the spring of 1873, when the heirs' children took possession of the estate, the laboratory and the Journal, which had by then grown to two and a half volumes.
>
> The village had grown. Where the wooden houses had stood there were half-timbered ones with painted beams, a paved street, a post office, two inns and a doctor. The priest was still Father Anzelm, older and thinner, but no less stubborn. And there was, as one of the new heirs wrote in a letter to a sister, "this thing they call the veil here, as if it were a matter of weather, like the rain or the fog".

> The telegram reached the new heirs in distant cities, in offices, laboratories and colleges. When they stepped off the train (for now the train went there too) they found a small town that no longer resembled the village of the family stories: street lamps along the main road, a telegraph office, a bank with columns of imitation marble and, in the café on the square, a phonograph that played Viennese waltzes for anyone who dropped in a coin.
